newsitem.title: PERU: Subdued New Year in Lima as 81 held by rebels.
newsitem.headline: Subdued New Year in Lima as 81 held by rebels.

text.p: A subdued New Year's Eve devoid of fireworks and festivity melted into one more day in captivity on Wednesday for 81 people held hostage by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

Inside the besieged building the only signs of merrymaking on Dec. 31 were the empty bottles and discarded plates of a gala reception stormed 15 days ago by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) to demand the release of 400 jailed colleagues, witnesses said.

Journalists who entered the compound on Tuesday described a scene like a ghost ship in the gardens of the residence, where a Dec. 17 reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito was gatecrashed by the rebels in a hail of bullets.
Wary of alarming the 20-odd heavily-armed rebels, Lima authorities had banned the usual cacophonous celebration of the New Year with rockets and fireworks in the swish San Isidro neighbourhood.

Reporters and police camped outside the residence twirled a few desultory sparklers at midnight but otherwise only the occasional explosion lit up the sky, and nothing that could be misinterpreted by the rebels as a armed assault.

New Year's Eve also appeared to dissolve chances of an early end to the stand-off, although the MRTA freed two more hostages -- Honduran ambassador Jose Eduardo Martell Mejia and Argentine consul general Juan Ibanez.
The releases followed what seemed to be a partly accidental propaganda coup for the rebels.

A group of journalists who had been allowed to approach the entrance of the residence to take photographs and video footage made a rush for the door and were allowed inside by MRTA members who, apparently fearful of undercover policemen, initially tried to shoo them away.
Once they were inside, MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, dressed in green military fatigues and covering his face with a red-and-white bandanna, gave an impromptu news conference.
Reversing what had seemed to be a softening of the rebel position over previous days, Cerpa said the rebels would not relax their demand for the release of their comrades.
"We are inflexible in our original position," Cerpa said. "I do not see an immediate solution."

He said the rebels were in "no hurry" to end the standoff, even though the group had left "the doors open" and was "open to any mediator ... (Cuban leader Fidel) Castro or (Russian President) Boris Yeltsin or whoever."
The rebels paraded their key hostage, Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, in front of reporters. A relaxed Tudela called for a peaceful solution to the crisis.
Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated cocktail party, was also brought before the cameras.
Looking grave and tired he offered apologies for the embassy's involvement in the crisis. "A thousand apologies from my government," he said in faltering Spanish.
Cerpa said the MRTA had already achieved its aim of drawing world attention to the bad conditions of Peruvian jails, and would now concentrate on obtaining the release of prisoners.
He said responsibility for resolving the crisis lay with the government. "There has been no opening up. This is now in the hands of the government. The government must reflect," Cerpa said.

Earlier in the week President Alberto Fujimori and his Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi had both struck a softer note than at the beginning of the crisis, saying they trusted the stand-off would be brought to a peaceful end.
But their tone was sharply undermined by Cerpa's comments and an earlier statement shouted by an unidentified rebel to the reporters outside the building.
The rebel slammed Fujimori's government as a "dictatorship dressed up as a democracy" practising "state terrorism that kills through starvation."

He shouted that the guerrillas were "determined to make the ultimate sacrifice" in the siege. "Any harm to them (the remaining hostages) will be the exclusive responsibility of the government of Mr Fujimori if he decides upon a military intervention."

Fujimori's appointed negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, met Cerpa on Saturday and achieved the release of 20 hostages, but no new meeting has taken place since. In all the rebels have released more than 420 hostages so far.
